sugestoes.texto: WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key copies the numeric Paginator implementation and calls math.floor/ceil on the raw key value. WHY: AuditLogEntry is ordered by '-datetime', so getattr(item, self.key) returns a datetime object and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError, crashing pagination for authorized users. HOW: Use DateTimePaginator-style conversion (strftime('%s.%f') * multiplier) before floor/ceil, or make OptimizedCursorPaginator inherit from DateTimePaginator.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor.value instead of converting it back to a datetime. WHY: BasePaginator.build_queryset compares this value against the datetime column in raw SQL, causing a type mismatch or wrong filter results when paging past the first page. HOW: Convert the numeric cursor value back to a timezone-aware datetime, matching DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor.

WHAT: The enable_advanced_features branch passes negative offsets directly to queryset[start_offset:stop]. WHY: Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indices, so any authorized admin cursor with a negative offset triggers an AssertionError instead of efficient reverse pagination. HOW: Remove the branch or implement negative-offset pagination with list slicing after evaluating the queryset, not on the QuerySet itself.

WHAT: The enable_advanced check dereferences organization_context.member without verifying it is not None. WHY: RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is typed as RpcOrganizationMember | None and documented as nullable when the user has no membership, so a non-superuser without membership triggers AttributeError. HOW: Guard the member access or combine the checks safely.

The endpoint selects OptimizedCursorPaginator when optimized_pagination=true, but that paginator's get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on the raw sort attribute. With order_by='-datetime' the key is a datetime object, so math.ceil will raise TypeError and break pagination for superusers/global-access members. Either use an integer/timestamp ordering compatible with OptimizedCursorPaginator, or make OptimizedCursorPaginator handle DateTime keys (e.g., like DateTimePaginator's timestamp conversion) before selecting it here.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses math.floor/math.ceil on `getattr(item, self.key)`, which requires a numeric value. However, organization_auditlogs.py instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is the datetime field and the value is a datetime object. This will raise TypeError at runtime when the paginator tries to build cursors. Either preserve the datetime-aware key logic used by DateTimePaginator, or restrict OptimizedCursorPaginator to numeric ordering fields and update the caller accordingly.

get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key). For the audit log endpoint order_by='-datetime', self.key is 'datetime' and the value is a datetime object, so math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError and the GET request crashes for any user with optimized_pagination=true. The sort key must be converted to a numeric timestamp (or use the same logic as DateTimePaginator) before floor/ceil is applied.

When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset is negative, the code passes the negative offset directly to queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django/Python slicing interprets a negative start index as "count from the end of the queryset", not as a negative offset from the start, so the returned page is the wrong set of rows and breaks pagination invariants. Negative offsets must be translated to a positive LIMIT/OFFSET query or bounded to zero.

The modified BasePaginator.get_result sets start_offset = offset (without max(0, ...)) when cursor.is_prev is true. If a prev cursor carries a negative offset, queryset[start_offset:stop] slices from the end of the queryset instead of paginating forward from the start, returning incorrect rows for the previous page path.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns cursor.value unchanged, while BasePaginator.value_from_cursor returns cursor.value + 1 for prev cursors. Since build_queryset uses this value as the pagination boundary, backward navigation will use an inclusive instead of exclusive boundary and can return the cursor row again or skip rows. Restore the prev-cursor increment or call the base implementation to keep boundary semantics consistent.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls getattr(item, self.key) directly and omits the callable-key branch that BasePaginator.get_item_key provides. This contradicts the docstring's claim of backward compatibility and will raise TypeError for any queryset ordered by a callable key. Add the same isinstance(self.key, Callable) branch used by BasePaginator.

OptimizedCursorPaginator uses `queryset[cursor.offset:cursor.offset+limit+extra]` when `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`. Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative start indices and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`, so this path will crash instead of providing efficient reverse pagination. Negative offsets need to be translated into a positive LIMIT/OFFSET query (or clamped/validated) before slicing the queryset.

Lines 875-879 claim 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indices and raises an AssertionError. Either remove the negative-offset branch or rewrite the comment to warn that negative offsets are unsupported by Django, and do not rely on the current claim.

The comment at lines 179-181 says negative offsets are allowed for bidirectional pagination, but line 182 computes `start_offset = max(0, offset) unless cursor.is_prev`, which clamps negative offsets to zero in the common forward-pagination case. Update the comment to describe the actual behavior, or change the code to match the documented intent.

The class docstring lists 'Optimized query path for large datasets' and 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', but the implementation largely duplicates BasePaginator.get_result and uses the same build_queryset path; it also adds extra conditional branches rather than streamlining boundary handling. Revise the docstring to describe only the features actually implemented (negative-offset branch when enable_advanced_features is true) and avoid claiming backward compatibility or query-path optimizations unless the code supports them.

The comments at lines 68-69 and 74-75 describe the new OptimizedCursorPaginator path as a 'Performance optimization' and 'high-performance audit log navigation'. Since OptimizedCursorPaginator does not contain a distinct optimized query path and is structurally equivalent to the base paginator with extra negative-offset handling, these comments mislead maintainers and API consumers. Update them to describe the actual change (gated cursor paginator with optional negative-offset behavior) or implement the claimed optimizations.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative cursor offsets straight into Django queryset slicing, which Django does not support, so requests with a negative offset raise an error instead of returning a page.
issues.textoGolden: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

comentarios.texto: The advanced negative-offset branch passes a negative slice start directly to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative indexing. A cursor such as 0:-1:0 is accepted by Cursor.from_string but crashes the optimized audit-log request instead of providing reverse pagination. Reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError or implement reverse traversal using nonnegative slices and reversed ordering.

The comment claiming that Django ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false: Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices. This branch passes cursor.offset straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], so it raises rather than supplying the documented negative-offset pagination. Correct the negative-offset support claims here, in the class docstring, and in the new BasePaginator boundary-handling comment (or implement actual supported boundary handling) so callers are not promised a pagination mode that the underlying queryset cannot provide.

Django QuerySets do not support negative slice bounds. Passing a negative cursor offset directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` raises an exception instead of enabling advanced pagination. Validate or normalize negative offsets before slicing, or implement reverse traversal through ordering/filtering rather than negative slices.

issues.descricao: The comment added to BasePaginator claims negative offsets are allowed and safely handled by the queryset, but the code clamps non-prev offsets to zero and leaves prev offsets as before, so the comment misdescribes the behaviour.

comentarios.texto: The added comment says this change will "allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination ... safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions", but the statement it annotates, line 182, is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` — it clamps negative offsets to 0, i.e. it does the opposite of what the comment claims and leaves the 'negative offset' (offset < 0) paging behaviour exactly as before. The comment is now untrue for the code it sits on; either drop the 'allow negative offsets' wording or make the code actually permit them.

The comment declares this change `allow[s] negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination`, but the actual computation is `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which clamps non-prev offsets at 0 — i.e. it never permits a negative offset. The declared optimization is a no-op relative to the original `queryset[offset:stop]`; the comment describes behavior the code does not have.

BasePaginator now passes the raw `offset` to the slice whenever `cursor.is_prev` is true (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). A negative offset from a user-supplied prev cursor therefore reaches `queryset[negative:stop]`, which Django rejects. This crashes every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. Fix: always use `max(0, offset)`, or validate the offset when the cursor is parsed.

issues.descricao: The OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring claims streamlined boundary handling, an optimized query path and backward compatibility that the implementation, a copy of BasePaginator plus a negative-offset branch, does not provide.

comentarios.texto: Docstring lists 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets', and 'maintaining backward compatibility', but get_result (845-886) is a copy of BasePaginator with only a negative-offset branch added — no streamlined handling or optimized path exists, and negative-offset slicing breaks prior cursor semantics. Doc describes behavior the function does not produce — align doc to code or implement the claimed handling.

issues.descricao: OptimizedCursorPaginator computes cursor keys with math.floor/ceil on the raw attribute, but the audit log endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so building the cursor raises TypeError for any non-empty result.
issues.textoGolden: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

comentarios.texto: OptimizedCursorPaginator requires numeric integer keys (get_item_key uses math.floor/ceil + int, cursor_value defaults to 0) but is instantiated here with order_by="-datetime". This mismatched producer/consumer contract breaks pagination for datetime-ordered audit logs. Fix: do not use OptimizedCursorPaginator for datetime ordering; keep DateTimePaginator or make OptimizedCursorPaginator datetime-aware.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key/value_from_cursor mishandles datetime ordering by calling math.floor/ceil directly on a datetime and returning raw int cursor value. WHY: Used with order_by="-datetime" it crashes with TypeError on floor(datetime) when building cursors and filters the datetime column against an int in build_queryset, breaking pagination. HOW: Copy DateTimePaginator logic — timestamp via strftime/multiplier with floor/ceil and convert cursor value back with datetime.fromtimestamp.

The optimized branch selects a numeric-key paginator while ordering by the datetime field. On any nonempty first page, build_cursor invokes OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, which calls math.ceil on a datetime and raises TypeError; nonzero cursors also lack the datetime conversion provided by DateTimePaginator. Make the optimized paginator inherit DateTimePaginator or preserve its timestamp encoding and decoding.

issues.descricao: The audit log endpoint always dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access, which crashes with AttributeError for authorized token requests that have no member, even on the default pagination path.
issues.textoGolden: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.

comentarios.texto: The unconditional advanced-access check dereferences organization_context.member although RpcUserOrganizationContext permits member=None. Authorized non-member organization-token requests therefore raise AttributeError even when optimized_pagination is absent, instead of returning audit logs through the existing paginator. Guard the optional member and evaluate eligibility only when optimized pagination is requested.

issues.descricao: The comments and enable_advanced variable describe the optimized_pagination path as a performance optimization for administrators, hiding that it enables negative-offset slicing.

comentarios.texto: The comments describe a 'performance optimization' for 'authorized administrators', and the variable is named enable_advanced. In fact it opts into negative-offset slicing, and the optimized_pagination query parameter gates it. The names and comments hide what the flag actually enables. Rename them to say what is enabled, or remove the path.

issues.descricao: A user-controlled optimized_pagination flag lets any member with global access switch to a paginator that accepts unvalidated negative cursor offsets, widening the attack surface and causing server errors.

comentarios.texto: A user-controlled `optimized_pagination` query flag switches the endpoint to a paginator that accepts attacker-supplied negative cursor offsets. This is available to any user with global access, not only to real admins. It widens the attack surface for unvalidated cursor offsets and causes server errors. The comment 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' is not backed by any check in the paginator. Fix: remove the optimized path, or have the paginator validate and clamp offsets.

issues.descricao: BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets only for next cursors; a prev cursor with a negative offset is passed straight into the queryset slice, which Django rejects with an error (500) on every paginated endpoint.
The new comment in Cursor says negative offsets are allowed to enable efficient reverse pagination, but the constructor only calls int(offset) and provides no such behaviour.
OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value, which is then compared against the datetime column, so next/prev cursor pagination of audit logs breaks.
Comments in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result claim Django handles negative slicing and that permissions are checked at the queryset level; both are false.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Any attendee of a booking is authorized to add arbitrary guests. WHY: An attendee who knows the bookingId can invoke addGuests and inject new recipients into a meeting they do not own, bypassing organizer control and exposing meeting links/calendar events to unintended parties. HOW: Restrict addGuests to the same principals as bookingsProcedure (organizer or collective participant) or gate attendee access behind an explicit organizer/team-admin permission.

WHAT: The team permission check requires the user to be both a team admin and a team owner. WHY: `isTeamAdmin` already returns true for ADMIN or OWNER roles; `isTeamOwner` returns true only for OWNER, so pure team admins are incorrectly denied permission to add guests. HOW: Change the operator from `&&` to `||` so either an admin or an owner is authorized.

WHAT: `sendAddGuestsEmails` receives the raw `guests` input instead of the deduplicated `uniqueGuests` list. WHY: If the request includes an email that is already an attendee, that attendee is filtered out of `uniqueGuests` and no new record is created, but the email logic still treats it as a new guest and sends `AttendeeScheduledEmail` instead of `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. HOW: Pass `uniqueGuests` to `sendAddGuestsEmails`.

WHAT: The blacklisted-guest check is case-sensitive. WHY: `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` is lowercased before comparison, but the submitted `guest` email is compared verbatim, so a blacklisted address submitted with different casing (e.g. `BadEmail@example.com`) is accepted. HOW: Normalize the submitted email to lowercase before comparing against the lowercased blacklist.

The onError handler concatenates err.data?.code and t(err.message) and shows it in a toast. If the server ever returns a raw error string instead of a translation key, sensitive details (emails, booking IDs, internal error text) could be exposed to the user. Defensively treat err.message as a key only when it is known to be a key, or fall back to a generic translation such as t("unable_to_add_guests") rather than rendering the server message directly.

The handler filters the input into `uniqueGuests` and persists only those, but then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original unfiltered array. Pass `uniqueGuests` instead so the email manager's `newGuests` parameter matches the attendees that were actually added.

The variable name and the authorization intent are 'admin OR owner', but the expression uses &&, so a team admin who is not also an owner (or vice versa) is incorrectly denied permission to add guests. Change && to ||.

The handler computes uniqueGuests (excluding existing attendees and blacklisted emails) to create the new attendees, but sendAddGuestsEmails receives the unfiltered guests list. That list is used to choose between AttendeeScheduledEmail and AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, so a duplicate email in the input will be treated as a new guest and existing attendees will receive the wrong template. Pass uniqueGuests instead.

When err.data?.code is undefined the template literal produces the literal string "undefined: ...", and because that string is truthy the friendly fallback t("unable_to_add_guests") is never shown. Only prepend the code when it exists, otherwise use the translated message or fallback.

The uniqueness refine uses `new Set(emails)`, which compares strings case-sensitively. Email addresses are case-insensitive identity data, so `A@example.com` and `a@example.com` pass validation as unique but refer to the same mailbox. Normalize emails with `toLowerCase()` before the Set comparison (and ideally persist the normalized form) to prevent case-variation duplicates and any downstream bypass of case-sensitive attendee or blacklist checks.

The variable `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is defined with `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, so a user must be both admin and owner to pass the check. The identifier says "or" and the surrounding permission logic at line 54 treats it as an either-or gate. Change `&&` to `||` so team admins or team owners can add guests, matching the name and intended behavior.

The `Tooltip` for removing an email field hardcodes `content="Remove email"`, bypassing the i18n system used elsewhere in the component. This text reaches the user untranslated. Pass it through the translation function, e.g., `content={t("remove_email")}`, and add the corresponding key to the locale files.

The error message is built as `` `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}` ``. The code portion is shown raw (and becomes "undefined:" when `err.data` is missing), so it is not localized and can be confusing. Because `message` is always truthy, the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback is never used. Build a fully localized message instead of concatenating an untranslated code, or use the translated fallback directly.

issues.descricao: isTeamAdminOrOwner combines isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner with &&, so only team owners pass; team admins who are not organizer or attendee are wrongly rejected with FORBIDDEN.
issues.textoGolden: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && instead of ||. WHY: isTeamAdmin returns truthy for role ADMIN or OWNER while isTeamOwner returns true only for OWNER, so the && expression is only true for OWNERs; team ADMINs are treated as unauthorized and get FORBIDDEN when adding guests, contradicting the variable's intent. HOW: use `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) || (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0))`.

The flag is named `isTeamAdminOrOwner` but is computed with `&&` (both admin AND owner). A team admin who is not the owner, or the owner who is not flagged admin, will fail this check, so the guard at line 54 wrongly throws FORBIDDEN for legitimate admins/owners. Use `||` between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner.

The variable `isTeamAdminOrOwner` names an OR condition, but the code combines `isTeamAdmin(...)` and `isTeamOwner(...)` with `&&`, so it is true only when the user is both admin AND owner. Either the name is wrong or the operator is; as written the permission check at line 54 denies a plain team admin, contradicting what the identifier promises. Use `||` to match the name (or rename if AND is intended).

issues.descricao: The guest blacklist is lowercased but incoming guest emails are compared without normalization, so a blacklisted address submitted with different casing bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS and is added and emailed.
issues.textoGolden: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The blacklist is compared case-sensitively against guest input while blacklistedGuestEmails are lowercased. WHY: blacklistedGuestEmails entries are lowercased but the filter compares `guest` verbatim (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`); an authenticated user can add a blacklisted address simply by changing its case (e.g. `Foo@bar.com` vs `foo@bar.com`), bypassing the configured BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restriction. HOW: normalize the guest before comparison, e.g. `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())`.

Case-sensitivity bypass of the guest blacklist. `blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased on the list side (line 71) but the input side is compared raw: `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` (line 77). A guest email submitted with any different casing (e.g. `Foo@Bar.com` when the blacklist holds `foo@bar.com`) passes the filter and is persisted, defeating BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS. Normalize the input before comparison, e.g. filter on `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())` (and likewise lowercase `guest` for the attendee dedup check).

WHAT: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entries are lowercased but the incoming guest string is compared without lowercasing/normalizing. WHY: an attacker bypasses the blocklist with case variation (e.g. Spam@Example.com) and gets added/emailed.

issues.descricao: The server never deduplicates the guests array, so a request with the same email twice inserts duplicate attendee rows for the booking.
issues.textoGolden: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: uniqueGuests filter only dedupes against existing booking.attendees with case-sensitive === and never dedupes duplicates within the input guests array itself (server schema has no uniqueness refine unlike the client). WHY: a request with the same new email twice creates duplicate attendee rows via createMany.

uniqueGuests filters only against existing attendees/blacklist but never dedupes guests[] itself and schema has no uniqueness check. A request like guests=[a@x.com,a@x.com] passes the filter twice and createMany inserts duplicate attendee rows or throws an unhandled DB unique-constraint exception. Dedupe/normalize input (and reject intra-request duplicates) before createMany.

uniqueGuests filters against existing attendees but does not deduplicate addresses within the incoming guests array. A direct mutation with the same new address twice inserts two Attendee records and sends duplicate invitations because the server schema permits duplicates and the Attendee model has no unique booking/email constraint. Deduplicate normalized input before filtering and inserting.

issues.descricao: Check-then-insert without a transaction or unique constraint lets two concurrent addGuests calls for the same email both pass the existing-attendee check and create duplicate attendees.

comentarios.texto: Race condition: findFirst check for existing attendees then booking.update+createMany is not atomic. Two concurrent addGuests calls with the same new email both see it as absent and both insert, creating duplicates. Guard with a unique constraint and handle conflict or run in a transaction/serializable check.

Check-then-insert race: the handler reads `booking.attendees` at the start, filters against it, then inserts in a separate `prisma.booking.update ... createMany` with no transaction or unique guard. Two concurrent addGuests calls for the same guest both see it as absent and both insert, producing duplicate attendees. Wrap the read+filter+insert in a transaction (or rely on a unique constraint on (bookingId, email) and handle the conflict) so concurrent requests cannot both succeed.

issues.descricao: Attendee authorization and existing-attendee dedup compare emails case-sensitively, so an attendee with differently-cased stored email is FORBIDDEN and a case-variant of an existing attendee is added again.

comentarios.texto: Inconsistent email normalization for identity checks. Both the authorization check `attendee.email === user.email` (line 52) and the existing-attendee dedup `guest === attendee.email` (line 76) use strict case-sensitive equality, while emails are treated as case-insensitive everywhere else in this handler (the blacklist block directly below lowercases). Consequence: a legitimate attendee whose stored casing differs from their session email is wrongly FORBIDDEN, and a guest differing from an existing attendee only by case is duplicated rather than filtered. Compare on a normalized form (both sides `.toLowerCase()`), consistent with the blacklist normalization.

issues.descricao: The handler passes the unfiltered guests list to sendAddGuestsEmails, which uses it to pick who gets AttendeeScheduledEmail, so existing attendees included in the request receive a new-booking confirmation instead of the add-guests email.
issues.textoGolden: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) passes the raw input guests instead of the filtered uniqueGuests. WHY: already-existing attendees included in the request are misclassified as newGuests in email-manager and receive AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail (wrong notification).

Dead-transform / wrong input: `uniqueGuests` is computed (dedup vs existing attendees + blacklist) and written to DB, but `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the original `guests`. Existing attendees re-submitted are then `includes()`-matched as new and get AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. Pass `uniqueGuests`.

Pass `uniqueGuests` (the filtered set written to DB) to sendAddGuestsEmails instead of raw `guests`; the email layer assumes newGuests exactly equals newly created attendees for its Scheduled vs AddGuests branch.

issues.descricao: EventManager is created with the requesting user's credentials, so when a non-organizer adds guests the organizer's calendar event is not updated (or the wrong account is used) for references without a credentialId.

comentarios.texto: EventManager is initialized with the requesting user's credentials rather than the booking organizer's credentials. When an attendee or team owner adds guests to a booking whose calendar reference lacks credentialId, updateAllCalendarEvents selects credentials by type from the caller's calendars, so the organizer's event is not updated or the update targets the wrong account. Load credentials for booking.userId and initialize the manager with the booking owner.

issues.descricao: Claims a failing calendar update at addGuests.handler.ts:165 aborts the mutation after guests are persisted; the calendar update path already swallows provider errors.

comentarios.texto: The attendees are written to the database at line 92, but `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` at line 165 runs outside the try/catch. If it throws, the mutation returns an error even though the guests are already persisted, so the DB and the calendar are out of sync. No emails are sent, and a retry then fails with 'emails_must_be_unique_valid'. Catch and handle the calendar update failure after the DB write.

The attendees are already committed to the DB when `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` is awaited without a try/catch. If the calendar sync throws, the mutation returns an error and skips the emails, although the guests were added. The caller sees a failure for a partly applied change and may retry. Handle calendar sync failure as best-effort, as the email send is, or run it before the DB write.

issues.descricao: Claims any attendee can add guests and trigger invites; this is the deliberate permission model of the new feature.

comentarios.texto: Any attendee, matched only by email, is allowed to add arbitrary guests to a booking, and the handler then sends emails and calendar invites on the organizer's behalf. Any attendee can use this to send invites to arbitrary addresses. Restrict the action to the organizer and team admins, or verify that the attendee's email is confirmed.

issues.descricao: The guests array has no server-side size limit, so any authorized caller, including an attendee, can add thousands of guests and trigger an unbounded batch of inserts and emails.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: guests is an unbounded z.array(z.string().email()) with no max length. WHY: any authorized caller (including a mere attendee) can submit thousands of emails causing unbounded createMany inserts plus unbounded Promise.all email fanout in sendAddGuestsEmails.

The mutation accepts an unbounded guest array that is persisted and immediately expanded into concurrent emails to every attendee. For non-seated bookings each email's ICS serializes the full attendee list, so adding N guests creates O(N) concurrent sends and O(N²) aggregate attachment work; repeated additions also resend to all existing attendees. Enforce a server-side guest-count and total-attendee limit before insertion and bound notification concurrency.

issues.descricao: The Remove email tooltip in MultiEmail is a hard-coded English string instead of a translation key.

comentarios.texto: Tooltip content="Remove email" is hard-coded English user-facing text bypassing i18n while surrounding strings in the same file/PR use t(). Wrap it in t() e.g. content={t("remove_email")} and add the key to locales.

`Tooltip content="Remove email"` is a hard-coded English user-facing string, while the surrounding code in this same component routes user text through `t()` (e.g. `t("add_another")` on line 69). This string bypasses the translation mechanism and will never be localised; it should use a translation key.

The new removal tooltip hard-codes `Remove email`, so users in non-English locales see English text even though the neighbouring controls use `t(...)` and this component already obtains `t` from useLocale. Route this tooltip through a translation key (and supply its English translation) rather than using the literal.

issues.descricao: The onError fallback to unable_to_add_guests is unreachable because the template-string message is always truthy.

comentarios.texto: Unreachable fallback: `message` is a template string `${code}: ${...}` which is always truthy, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never takes the fallback. Build message conditionally or test the underlying parts for emptiness.

In `onError`, `message` is always a non-empty template string (`"${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}"`), so the fallback `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` is unreachable and the newly added `unable_to_add_guests` translation is never shown. The user is instead shown a raw error code prefix like `BAD_REQUEST: ...` rather than the translated message; the fallback and code prefix handling should be corrected so the intended translated text reaches the user.

The error message is built as a template string, so it is always truthy. The `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback is therefore dead code, and the user can see "undefined: ..." or an untranslated raw message. Use `err.message ? t(err.message) : t("unable_to_add_guests")`.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Backup code verification compares the user-supplied code without normalizing case. WHY: Generated backup codes are lowercase hex, so a user who types an otherwise valid code in uppercase is rejected as incorrect. HOW: Lower-case the stripped input before comparing, e.g. `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "").toLowerCase()`, and apply the same normalization in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61.

WHAT: The new backup-code authentication branch does not itself verify the user's password. WHY: Password verification is gated by `!credentials.totpCode`, so an attacker who knows a backup code can bypass the password by also sending any non-empty totpCode and authenticate successfully. HOW: Verify the password inside the backup-code branch (or move password verification before the second-factor branches) before consuming the backup code.

WHAT: The clipboard writeText call is not awaited and its errors are not handled. WHY: The success toast is shown immediately even if the browser rejects the copy (permission denied, insecure context, etc.), misleading the user and leaving an unhandled promise rejection. HOW: Await the clipboard call and only show the toast on success, or catch errors and show an error toast.
The component is exported as `TwoFactor` but the file is `BackupCode.tsx` and is imported as `BackupCode`. Rename the function to `BackupCode` so the identifier matches the file name and usage.

The assertion `await expect(page.locator(`[data-testid=two-factor-switch]`).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes even when the switch is not checked because `locator.isChecked()` returns a Promise, and a Promise object is always truthy when passed to the generic `toBeTruthy()` matcher. The PR added a FIXME noting this exact failure mode but left the assertion in place. Replace it with `await expect(page.locator(`[data-testid=two-factor-switch]`)).toBeChecked()` or `await expect(await page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBe(true)` so the test actually fails when the switch is unchecked.

If the clipboard write fails or writes the wrong text, the toast still appears and the test passes. Read the clipboard (e.g., `await page.evaluate(() => navigator.clipboard.readText())`) and assert it contains the expected backup codes.

The backup-code comparison uses `backupCodes.indexOf(...replaceAll("-", ""))`, which short-circuits on mismatch and leaks timing information about the stored secret codes. Replace it with a constant-time comparison over every code (e.g., `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) and decide the match only after the loop, so an attacker cannot learn which code is correct or how much of it they guessed.

The disable endpoint locates the supplied backup code with `backupCodes.indexOf(...replaceAll("-", ""))`. This performs a non-constant-time secret comparison and can leak information through response timing. Compare every stored code with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` and only return success/failure after evaluating all candidates.

issues.descricao: The credentials authorize() skips the password check when any totpCode is present, and the new backup-code branch never validates that totpCode, so a backup code plus a dummy totpCode logs in without the account password.

comentarios.texto: The new backup-code branch authenticates without guaranteeing the password check ran: password verification at line 121 is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, and the branch at line 131 triggers on any truthy `credentials.backupCode` regardless of that gate. A POST to the credentials callback supplying a valid backup code together with any non-empty totpCode therefore takes the backup branch (skipping TOTP validation) while line 121 skips password verification — granting a session using only a second-factor backup code, with no account password. Require the password check before the backup branch, or include backupCode in the guard at line 121 (e.g. `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode && !credentials.backupCode)`).

The backup-code branch accepts a valid backup code even when an arbitrary nonempty totpCode has skipped password verification. The preceding guards at lines 113–125 trust the presence of totpCode, but this new branch does not validate it, allowing a holder of a backup code to log in to a password account without knowing its password by submitting both fields. Require password verification for backup-code authentication rather than allowing an unverified totpCode to bypass it.

WHAT: The new backup-code login branch authenticates without verifying the password when credentials also contain any totpCode value (password check at line 121 is skipped when totpCode is truthy, and the backup branch never checks it). WHY: An attacker holding only a backup code can add a dummy totpCode to the credentials callback and log in without the password, reducing two factors to one. HOW: Verify the password whenever backupCode is used (or decouple the password check from totpCode presence).

If the user dismisses the Dialog via ESC or an overlay click, DialogContent's onOpenChange fires (wired to a plain setEnableModalOpen toggle at apps/web/pages/settings/security/two-factor-auth.tsx:64 and the conditional render at apps/web/components/security/TwoFactorAuthSection.tsx:36), so onEnable never runs. The parent callbacks (setEnableModalOpen(false) + utils.viewer.me.invalidate() / setEnabled(true)) are skipped, leaving the 2FA Switch unchecked and the UI showing 2FA as disabled even though the server has enabled it. Call onEnable() from the dismiss path (onOpenChange) or when transitioning into DisplayBackupCodes, not only from the Close button.

Successful enablement no longer invokes onEnable until the backup-code screen's explicit Close button is clicked. Dismissing that screen through the dialog's onOpenChange instead only closes it in the parent and does not invalidate viewer.me, leaving the settings switch showing disabled even though the server has enabled 2FA. Ensure dismissal after successful enablement also invokes the completion callback and resets the setup state.

After a successful enable, `onEnable()` is no longer called and is only called from the backup-codes Close button. If the user dismisses the dialog by Escape or overlay click (`onOpenChange`) while the codes are displayed, the parent is never notified that 2FA is enabled. The modal also keeps its step state and the plaintext backup codes. Call `onEnable` when 2FA is enabled, or make the dialog's `onOpenChange(false)` on the DisplayBackupCodes step run the same handler as Close, which resets state and clears `backupCodes`.

issues.descricao: Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent logins can accept the same backup code more than once or overwrite each other's removal.
issues.textoGolden: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

comentarios.texto: Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write: the code is validated with indexOf (line 144) and only then persisted via prisma.user.update (line 149), with no unique constraint or lock. Two concurrent login requests sending the same valid backup code both read the unchanged row, both pass the indexOf check, and both obtain a session, violating the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' invariant. Consume the code atomically (e.g. a conditional update on the raw encrypted value / a dedicated used-backup-codes table with a unique index) so only one request can succeed.

Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, breaking the stated invariant that each backup code is single-use. Two concurrent login requests with the same backup code both read the same user.backupCodes array and both pass `index !== -1` before either `prisma.user.update` commits; both then persist a stale array (each nulling only its own index), so the code authenticates twice. Make consumption atomic (e.g. compare-and-swap on the encrypted value/updatedAt, a transaction with a conditional update, or an optimistic-locking retry) so exactly one request can claim a given code.

Backup-code consumption overwrites the encrypted list by user ID without checking that the stored list still matches the value read before verification. Concurrent requests can both authenticate with the same single-use code, and requests using different codes can overwrite each other's removals and restore a consumed code. Use a conditional atomic update matching the original backupCodes ciphertext and reject or retry authentication if no row was updated.

enableSqlExpressions ignores the feature flag it checks and always returns false. The function computes whether FlagSqlExpressions is NOT enabled, then returns false in both branches, so SQL expressions are rejected even when the flag is turned on. It should return the actual flag state, e.g. `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`.

The `enableSqlExpressions` helper is logically inverted/buggy: it computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns `false` in both branches. sugestoes.texto: WHAT: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but the pool is created and owned by ResultsStrategyFactory. WHY: Arroyo calls strategy.close() on partition revocation and factory.shutdown() at consumer shutdown; closing a per-strategy object destroys the factory's shared pool, so subsequent create_with_partitions() calls reuse a dead pool and the factory.shutdown() double-closes it. HOW: Remove self.queue_pool.shutdown() from close()/terminate() in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy and let ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() manage the pool lifecycle, matching parallel_executor.

WHAT: The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing", but OrderedQueueWorker.run() calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in a finally block even when result_processor raises an exception. WHY: Offsets for failed messages are marked complete and will be committed as soon as all prior contiguous offsets finish, breaking the documented guarantee. If the intent is truly to skip failed offsets, move complete_offset out of finally and only call it on success (or add an explicit failure tracker).

WHAT: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that no offsets are committed after a processing failure, but the implementation completes offsets for failed items in a finally block and then commits past them. WHY: The test will be flaky/incorrect because both offsets 100 and 101 complete, so get_committable_offsets() will return offset 101 (committed as 102 by commit_offsets). The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` will fail whenever the commit loop wakes up before the assertion. Align the test with the intended semantics: either expect commit offset 102 (move past failures) or change the implementation to not complete failed offsets.

WHAT: FixedQueuePool creates unbounded queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize. WHY: The docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but put() never blocks, so when ingestion outpaces processing the queues grow without bound and can consume unbounded memory. HOW: Pass maxsize=N to queue.Queue() and rely on the blocking put() to apply backpressure, or document that backpressure must come from the upstream Arroyo strategy.

WHAT: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets() iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) to find the highest contiguous completed offset. WHY: If offsets are sparse (log-compacted topic, skipped filtered messages), the loop runs in O(offset gap) rather than O(backlog), which can become very large and stalls the commit thread. HOW: Sort the tracked offsets and walk the sorted list to find the highest contiguous completed offset, which is O(n log n) in the number of tracked offsets.
