issues.descricao: Claims OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets requires every integer offset to exist, so Kafka offset gaps permanently block commits for the partition and per-partition state is never cleared on rebalance.

comentarios.texto: Offsets are only tracked for messages that were submitted, and there is no partition revoke handling. Contiguity is checked with `range(start, max_offset+1)`, so any offset gap (compacted topics, transactional markers, or offsets filtered out upstream) permanently blocks commits for that partition. The `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` state is never cleared on rebalance, so stale state survives partition reassignment. Treat gaps as committable once all lower tracked offsets are complete, and clear per-partition state when partitions are revoked.

The commit scan assumes consecutive Kafka offsets and breaks at the first offset that is not in all_offsets. A permanent offset gap (compacted or transactional records) then blocks commits for that partition forever. Track the submitted offsets in sorted order and commit up to the highest offset below the lowest outstanding one, rather than requiring every integer in between to be present.

Determine the commit boundary from received offsets rather than requiring every integer in this range to exist. Kafka offsets need not be consecutive: if 100, 102 and 103 are delivered and completed, this scan stops at the nonexistent 101 even though there is no unfinished record. Conversely, after committing 100 and removing it, the next scan starts at 102 and commits past the gap, contradicting the added gap tests. Iterate received offsets in sorted order and stop at the first outstanding record; add a test covering legitimate skipped Kafka offsets across multiple commit cycles.

issues.descricao: OrderedQueueWorker marks a work item's offset complete in a finally block even when processing raised, so failed messages are committed and dropped, contradicting the documented guarantee of committing only after successful processing.

comentarios.texto: The worker marks the offset complete in the `finally` block even when `result_processor(...)` raises, so a message whose handling failed is reported as committable and its offset is committed (it will never be retried). This contradicts the strategy's own guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, which asserts the partition is not committed after a failure. Only call `complete_offset` on the success path (or track failed offsets separately) so failures are not silently skipped.

The worker marks the offset complete in `finally` even when `result_processor` raised an exception, so a failed item's offset is reported as committable and gets committed by the commit loop. This contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and the contract asserted in test_results_consumer.py (test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, which expects the failed partition NOT to be committed): the failed message is committed past and never retried. Track success separately and only call `complete_offset` when processing succeeded (or make the failure explicit so the offset is withheld/retried).

The failed item's offset is completed unconditionally in the `finally` block, so `complete_offset` runs even when `result_processor` raised. This breaks the class's documented guarantee ('Only commits offsets after successful processing', line 254): the commit loop then advances past a message that was never successfully processed, silently dropping it (and, per the PR's own test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling, a commit is produced where none is expected). Only call `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` on the success path (i.e. after `result_processor` returns normally), or explicitly decide and document the at-most-once semantics; do not complete on the exception path.

issues.descricao: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling's docstring says errors must not block commits for other messages, but the test asserts that nothing was committed, so it does not verify the behaviour it describes.
issues.textoGolden: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

comentarios.texto: The commit assertion contradicts the test's own docstring and cannot fail for the reason it claims. The docstring says "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the body asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` — i.e. it passes only when nothing is committed. In queue_consumer.py ordered worker's `finally` calls `complete_offset` even after result_processor raises (lines 148-149), so offset 100 should be committable and offset 101 should advance the commit; if the whole commit path were removed (commits blocked entirely) the test would still pass. Assert the positive behaviour instead: e.g. that the failing message's offset was still completed so commits progressed (expect `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`, matching the follow-on offset of the successfully processed message).

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling claims errors don't block commits but asserts len(committed)==0 / not in, and waits only for total==0+sleep(0.2) while commit loop is 1.0s. It passes if commits are correctly made (checked before loop fires) and if commits are never made. Wait for commit condition and assert contiguous commit includes both offsets despite the exception.

issues.descricao: The error-handling test asserts no commit happened after only a 0.2s sleep while the commit loop runs every second, so it passes without ever observing whether a failed offset gets committed.

comentarios.texto: The error-handling test can pass even when failed messages are committed. It waits for two processor calls, sleeps only 0.2 seconds, and asserts that no commit has happened, whereas _commit_loop waits 1 second. OrderedQueueWorker currently completes the failed offset in finally, so the unsafe commit can occur after this assertion. Synchronize with an actual commit-loop iteration before asserting that it cannot advance past the failed offset.

issues.descricao: FixedQueuePool uses unbounded queues and the strategy never applies backpressure, so when workers fall behind the consumer keeps polling and queued work items grow memory without limit, contrary to the documented backpressure guarantee.

comentarios.texto: Each worker queue is created unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize) although the class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' and the strategy claims to guarantee backpressure. With no bound and no MessageRejected raised from submit(), a slow group continues to accumulate items in its queue while the consumer keeps polling, so memory grows without limit under a sustained backlog — the opposite of the intended protection. Fix: give the queues a maxsize and raise/return MessageRejected (or otherwise propagate backpressure to the caller) when a queue is full.

The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues this strategy drives are unbounded: `FixedQueuePool` creates each one as `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize (line 185), and `submit()` puts items unconditionally. Nothing ever blocks, so no backpressure exists. Either bound the queues (pass a `maxsize` and handle `queue.Full` / block in `submit`) or correct the docstring so it does not advertise a guarantee the code does not provide.

The pool creates unbounded queues, while strategy submit always accepts messages and poll never applies backpressure. When a queue's worker is slow or ingestion exceeds processing capacity, queued WorkItems retain both decoded results and original Kafka messages without any limit, causing growing memory consumption and eventual consumer OOM. Bound queued/in-flight work and raise Arroyo MessageRejected when capacity is reached, ensuring that rejection is not swallowed by the generic submit exception handler.

issues.descricao: Graceful shutdown sets each worker's shutdown flag before draining, so workers stop with items still queued, and close() stops the commit thread first, so finished work is not committed and gets replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True while OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on while not self.shutdown, so workers exit without draining queued WorkItems even though queues are shut down with immediate=False. WHY: Graceful shutdown silently drops queued items and leaves their offsets in outstanding forever, causing reprocessing/duplicates and failing the claimed graceful-shutdown guarantee. HOW: Remove the shutdown-flag short-circuit and let workers drain until queue.ShutDown, e.g. loop unconditionally and break only on ShutDown.

close() stops the commit thread and shuts down workers before draining accepted work, and join() only repeats close() instead of waiting for processing and making a final commit. Pool shutdown sets worker.shutdown before workers can drain their queues, so assignment revocation abandons queued results and completed in-flight work is not finally committed, causing replay and allowing unfinished old work to overlap a new owner. Make close() stop acceptance without blocking, then have join() drain accepted work within its timeout and commit completed offsets before releasing workers.

Do not set worker.shutdown before draining the queues during graceful shutdown. If a worker is processing A while B is queued, shutdown sets the flag; after A finishes, the worker exits at `while not self.shutdown` without ever retrieving B. Calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False) does not override that loop condition. Drain accepted work before stopping workers, and keep committing available until that drain completes; currently close stops the commit thread before the workers as well, so even work finished during shutdown is not finally committed.

issues.descricao: The strategy's close() shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool, so after a partition rebalance the next strategy reuses a dead pool; submissions fail and the error handler marks their offsets complete, committing messages that were never processed.

comentarios.texto: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is a singleton owned by the factory (created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and never recreated). Arroyo calls strategy.close() then join() on every assignment revocation/rebalance, and the factory's create_with_partitions is called again for the next assignment; the new strategy then reuses the already-shut-down queue_pool. Because q.shutdown(immediate=False) makes subsequent put() raise queue.ShutDown, submit()'s except branch (lines 317-325) swallows it and marks the offset complete, so after any rebalance every message is committed as processed without ever being handled — silent data loss. Fix: either let the factory own the pool lifecycle (don't shut it down from the strategy's close) and create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions, or reset/recreate factory.queue_pool when the strategy is closed.

WHAT: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate shuts down the factory-owned shared FixedQueuePool. WHY: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one queue_pool and hands it to every strategy from create_with_partitions, so Arroyo rebalance (close old strategy, create new one reusing factory.queue_pool) reuses a dead pool with joined workers and shut-down queues, stalling all further processing. HOW: Make pool lifecycle owned only by the factory: strategy close should only stop its commit thread, not call queue_pool.shutdown().

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close(), terminate() and join() shut down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is created once by ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy it creates. After a rebalance, Arroyo closes the old strategy and then calls create_with_partitions again, which reuses the dead pool. Messages then fail to enqueue, and the submit() exception handler marks them complete, so their offsets get committed without the messages being processed. The strategy should only stop its own commit thread. The pool should be shut down only by factory.shutdown(), or the pool should be created per strategy.

issues.descricao: The strategy invokes Arroyo's commit callback from a background thread rather than from submit/poll on the consumer thread, so commits can race with polling and partition revocation on a non-thread-safe consumer.

comentarios.texto: `commit_function` is called from the background commit thread, but arroyo's commit callback is expected to be called from the main consumer thread, and the Kafka consumer is not thread-safe. Committing from another thread risks races with polling and with rebalances.

issues.descricao: The WorkItem docstring says the original message is kept for offset tracking, but offset tracking only uses partition and offset and the message field is never used.

comentarios.texto: The `WorkItem` docstring says it "includes the original message for offset tracking", but the `message` field is never used for offset tracking — `OffsetTracker` and the commit loop only ever read `partition`/`offset`, and `submit()` even re-derives the offset from `message.value` rather than from the stored `message`. Update the docstring to describe what the field is actually for (or remove the unused field) so it does not misdescribe the dataclass contract.

`WorkItem.message` is declared with the comment 'includes the original message for offset tracking' and is populated in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, but nothing ever reads it — offset tracking uses the separate `partition`/`offset` fields. The declared purpose does not match any actual use, so the field (and the extra reference to each Kafka message it keeps alive) is dead; either use it for offset tracking or remove it.

issues.descricao: The tests named for concurrent processing across groups only check that all items were processed and all groups seen, so a fully serial implementation would pass and concurrency is never verified.

comentarios.texto: Test named/docstringed "Test that different groups are processed concurrently" never verifies concurrency. The body only asserts all 6 items ran and that three distinct group numbers were seen — a single worker draining one queue, or a fully serial FixedQueuePool, would satisfy both assertions. Either measure actual overlap (e.g. have result_processor block on a barrier/event until all three groups have entered, and fail on timeout) or drop the concurrency claim from the name/docstring.

test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions claims to verify that different subscriptions are processed concurrently, but the only assertion is `mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`, which a strictly serial implementation also satisfies. Add a real concurrency signal (e.g. a barrier in the mocked processor that requires both calls to be in flight simultaneously before either returns), otherwise this test cannot detect loss of parallelism.

test_concurrent_processing_across_groups claims concurrent processing but only asserts 6 items processed and 3 groups seen. A serial/single-queue implementation would still pass. Verify overlap (blocking processor + timing/thread IDs) or remove concurrency claim.

issues.descricao: The strategy ordering test submits identical messages and only checks the count processed, so it cannot detect out-of-order processing within a group.

comentarios.texto: The strategy ordering test submits five identical decoded results for sub1 and only asserts their count. Processing them in reverse order would still pass. Give each message a distinguishable sequence value and assert the exact processed sequence, so this tests ordering through SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy rather than only delivery.

issues.descricao: The graceful-shutdown test only asserts that the factory cleared its queue_pool reference, which shutdown always does, so it does not verify that pending work is drained or workers stop.

comentarios.texto: This does not verify graceful shutdown: factory.shutdown unconditionally clears queue_pool after calling pool.shutdown, so the assertion passes even if pending messages are abandoned or worker threads remain alive. Retain the pool reference and assert that all submitted work completed and its workers stopped; the current worker shutdown flag can stop workers without draining their queues.

issues.descricao: The polling bound max_wait = 50 is repeated as a magic number across the thread-queue-parallel tests instead of a named constant.
issues.textoGolden: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

issues.descricao: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets starts scanning at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset); after mark_committed prunes offsets, a gap is skipped on the next cycle, so offsets are committed past a missing offset, contrary to the 'highest contiguous offset' guarantee.
The test's wait loop stops at the first recorded commit but asserts the committed offset is exactly 105, so a commit fired mid-processing can record a lower offset and make the test flaky.
The per-worker queue_depth gauge is tagged only with identifier, so all queues report into one series and the metric shows whichever queue reported last.
SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate signals the commit thread without joining it, so the background thread is claimed to keep committing offsets for revoked partitions after terminate.
SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy passes FilteredPayload to decode_payload, whose assert raises instead of returning None, so filtered messages go through the error path.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: credentialModelOpt.get() is called without checking isPresent(), so a missing recovery-codes credential in both federated and local storage throws NoSuchElementException. WHY: This crashes the login form rendering when the credential is absent, instead of failing gracefully or redirecting to setup. HOW: Check credentialModelOpt.isPresent() before .get(), and throw a meaningful runtime exception or redirect if the credential is missing.

WHAT: After resolving a credential through RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, the code removes an exhausted credential via authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...), which only removes locally stored credentials. WHY: When the credential lives in federated/user storage, removeStoredCredentialById cannot remove it, so the exhausted credential remains and the user is stuck with an unremovable credential or spurious re-configuration prompts. HOW: Distinguish federated vs local credentials; for federated credentials invoke disableCredentialType(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE) or route removal through the user storage provider instead of removeStoredCredentialById.

WHAT: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes to JSON and passes them as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user storage, while the local-storage path stores hashed codes through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider. WHY: A user storage provider that persists the CredentialInput value (as the test BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does) stores recovery codes in plain text, exposing high-value backup credentials if the external store or its backups are compromised. HOW: Pass the codes in a form that lets the storage provider hash them before persistence, or document that user storage providers must hash the value themselves and update the test provider to hash before storing and compare hashed values during validation.

The recovery code verification uses direct String.equals() on hashed secrets, which is vulnerable to timing attacks. Use a constant-time comparison function (e.g., MessageDigest.isEqual) to compare the hashed input against each stored hashed recovery code.

The recovery key validation compares raw input recovery codes against stored values using key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()) inside a stream, which performs a non-constant-time comparison and leaks timing information. Use a constant-time comparison function for each candidate recovery code.

createRecoveryCodesCredential passes the raw generatedCodes JSON to user storage via updateCredential, while falling back to the credentialModel (which holds hashed codes) for local storage. This creates a representation split: user-storage providers receive and typically store plaintext recovery codes, whereas the local DB provider stores hashed codes. The validation path in the test user storage then compares raw input to raw stored codes, inconsistent with the normal hashed validation. The method should pass equivalent credential material to both paths, e.g., by using the credential model's serialized/hashed data for user storage as well, or by documenting and enforcing that user-storage providers must hash the received codes.

issues.descricao: The test user-storage provider validates recovery codes without consuming the used code, so the same code can be replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

The new recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list without consuming the accepted code. Repeating a successful login with the same code succeeds indefinitely, while getCredentials reconstructs all original codes so the login form never advances or detects exhaustion. Validate the next unused code and persist its consumption before returning success.

The new federated recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list but never removes a successfully used code from myUser.recoveryCodes. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid on subsequent logins, and getCredentials reconstructs the full original set every time. Consume and persist the successfully validated code (and test a second login/replay), so federated recovery codes retain their one-time semantics.

issues.descricao: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-codes credential without copying the stored credential id, so the returned federated credential has a null id and cannot be targeted by id-based removal.
issues.textoGolden: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code model without copying the ID assigned during updateCredential. createFromValues does not assign an ID, so the exposed federated credential has a null ID and CredentialDeleteHelper cannot resolve it by the stored credential ID for account deletion. Copy myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() to the reconstructed model before returning it.

The CredentialModel returned from getCredentials for recovery codes is built with createFromValues and never gets the stored credential's id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()). RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator later calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId()) once all codes are used, and this would pass a null id. Fix: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after creating the model.

issues.descricao: Creating recovery codes in external storage does not remove a previously stored local recovery-codes credential, and validation falls back to local storage, so the replaced codes still authenticate.

comentarios.texto: Successful recovery-code creation in external storage leaves any existing locally stored recovery-code credential active. For a federated user who previously stored codes locally and now has an external provider supporting this type, regeneration no longer calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential's replacement cleanup; UserCredentialManager.isValid falls back to the local validator when external validation rejects an old code, so the supposedly replaced codes still authenticate. Remove the previous local recovery-code credential after successful external creation.

issues.descricao: Exhausted recovery codes are removed with removeStoredCredentialById, which only covers local storage, so a federated recovery-codes credential is never removed.

comentarios.texto: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but this code still calls removeStoredCredentialById() on it once all codes are used. That removal only targets local stored credentials, so a federated credential may not be removed. The user could then be left with an exhausted credential in user storage. Remove federated credentials through the federated path, or confirm the removal reaches user storage.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a credential from user storage, but exhausted codes are cleaned up with removeStoredCredentialById, which only targets the local DB. For a federated credential (possibly with a null id), the exhausted credential is never removed or the call misbehaves, so the user keeps a dead credential. Remove federated credentials through a path that covers user storage, for example by checking where the credential came from.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a federated credential. The authenticator still removes an exhausted one with removeStoredCredentialById(getId()), which only deletes from the local store, and the federated model's id may be null. Remove the credential through the path that matches where it was found, for example by checking whether it came from the federated stream and using the federated removal.

issues.descricao: Looking up recovery codes now always queries the federated provider first, which for LDAP users adds an LDAP round-trip and can throw IllegalStateException, failing recovery-code login with a 500.
An error log in the test user storage hard-codes the credential type as 'recovery-codes' instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE ('recovery-authn-codes').

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The denial cache key concatenates resource name and parent folder using `_` separators without escaping them. WHY: A resource named `x_y` inside folder `z` produces the same key as a resource named `x` inside folder `y_z`, so a denial for one resource can be incorrectly returned for the other. HOW: Encode or escape underscores in `name` and `parent` before building the key, or use a structured key format (e.g., JSON/protobuf) that cannot collide.

WHAT: The denial cache stores negative authorization decisions for `shortCacheTTL` (30 seconds) and is never invalidated. WHY: If a user is denied access, then an admin grants permission to that exact resource, subsequent Check calls hit the cached denial and return false until the TTL expires, contradicting the PR goal of letting users access newly authorized dashboards and folders. HOW: Invalidate the matching denial cache entry whenever the user's permissions for the action are refreshed or updated; alternatively, skip denial caching for wildcard-capable actions or reduce the TTL if invalidation is not feasible.

WHAT: When permissions are found in the permission cache but `checkPermission` returns false, the code increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label `false` as if the cache missed. WHY: This metric conflates actual cache misses with cache hits that did not grant access, making cache-hit observability inaccurate. HOW: Increment the cache-usage metric with `true` immediately after a successful `getCachedIdentityPermissions` return, before evaluating whether the permission grants access.

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with only underscores as separators. Grafana folder/dashboard UIDs can contain underscores, so different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key (e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" vs name="a", parent="b_c"). A collision makes the denial cache return a false denial for a different resource. Use an unambiguous encoding such as null-byte delimiters or a hash of the components.

Check consults permDenialCache before the permission cache and DB, and only writes to it when the DB lookup denies. If a user's permissions change from deny to allow, the stale denial entry remains for the cache TTL and continues to deny access even though the current permission set would grant it. Either delete the denial entry when a Check finally allows, or avoid negative caching in the authorization path.

issues.descricao: The denial cache key joins name and parent folder with underscores, so different name/parent pairs can collide and a cached denial for one resource denies another until TTL expiry.
issues.textoGolden: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

comentarios.texto: The denial cache key does not distinguish underscores inside resource and parent UIDs from its field separators. For the same namespace, user and action, (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") generate the same key, so denying the first request makes Check return false for the second even if its permissions explicitly allow it. Encode the components unambiguously, for example as a JSON tuple or length-prefixed fields.

The denial cache key is not injective: for the same namespace, user and action, `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same key. After the first request stores a denial, Check's new early cache return denies the second request without checking its permissions, even if it is allowed. Encode the components unambiguously (for example a JSON tuple or length-prefixed components) and add a test verifying that these two requests do not share a denial entry.

Make the denial-cache key encode component boundaries unambiguously (for example, length-prefix or serialize the components). For the same namespace, user and action, name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` both produce the suffix `_a_b_c`. Underscores can occur in resource UIDs, so denying the first request caches a key that causes Check to immediately deny the second request without evaluating its permissions, even if that resource is allowed.

issues.descricao: The explicit denial-cache test seeds the cached permission as false instead of true, so it would pass without the denial-cache short-circuit and does not verify it.
issues.textoGolden: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

comentarios.texto: This test claims to prove the permDenialCache short-circuit (service.go:116-121) denies access, but it seeds the cached permission as map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} (a deny), contradicting its comment "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". Because the cached set is already a deny, checkPermission returns allowed=false, the code falls through to the DB path, and the fake store also returns no permissions, so Allowed stays false. The assertion passes even if the entire permDenialCache early-return were deleted. Seed the cached permission as true (map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}) so that only the denial-cache entry can force Allowed=false; otherwise the test does not verify the feature.

The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code sets the permCache entry to `false`, which is a deny. The test therefore does not show that the permission cache is skipped. Set the value to `true`, or change the comment to match.

The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test would still pass if the permDenialCache check were removed. permCache is seeded with dash1:false, not true as the comment claims, so the normal path also denies. Seed permCache with {"dashboards:uid:dash1": true} and a store that grants the permission, so Allowed=false can only come from the denial entry.

issues.descricao: A cached permission set that denies a resource always triggers a full DB permission reload, so checks over many inaccessible dashboards issue one query per resource instead of being served from cache.

comentarios.texto: Every distinct resource denied by the cached permission map triggers a reload of the entire user's action permission set, because the denial cache is resource-specific and a cached false result always falls through to getIdentityPermissions. Sequential checks of N inaccessible dashboards therefore execute N full permission queries and cache rewrites even with a current action-wide cache; getUserPermissions' singleflight only merges overlapping requests. Bound refreshes per user/action with a short refresh cooldown or generation marker so different resource misses can share a recent refresh.

issues.descricao: The Service struct comment listing its caches was not updated for the new permDenialCache field.

comentarios.texto: The struct doc comment still reads "// Cache for user permissions, user team memberships and user basic roles", but this PR added the new `permDenialCache` field (line 58). The comment no longer enumerates what the struct actually holds and misleads a reader about the new denial-cache field; update it to mention the permission-denial cache so the prose matches the fields.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Removing the coarse cacheMu lock at the start of BuildIndex leaves concurrent calls for the same NamespacedResource key unsynchronized. WHY: Two goroutines that reach BuildIndex for the same key (e.g., concurrent Search requests or a Search racing with a watch event via getOrCreateIndex) both create indexes; for file-backed indexes they collide on the same directory, and the second writer overwrites the first in the cache without closing it, leaking the index. HOW: Reintroduce per-key synchronization that still allows different keys to build concurrently—check the cache under a per-key lock/mutex before starting, return the existing index if present, and only write the newly built index if no other builder won the race.

NewResourceServer now invokes s.Init(ctx) during construction (lines 258-262), which is a behavioral contract change: construction previously returned a server that still required a separate Init call. Any consumer that calls Init after construction would be affected, though no such consumer-side breakage is visible in the changed code in this diff.

issues.descricao: BuildIndex now locks only the final cache assignment, so concurrent callers for the same uncached key all build the same expensive index in parallel and the last one overwrites the others.
issues.textoGolden: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Removing the function-wide `b.cacheMu.Lock()/defer Unlock()` and keeping only the lock around `b.cache[key]=idx` removes the only thing that serialized GetIndex against an in-flight build. WHY: getOrCreateIndex (resource/search.go:287-307) does GetIndex -> if nil -> build; previously BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole body so a concurrent caller's GetIndex (RLock) blocked until the first build cached the index and then saw it (no second build). Now GetIndex can return nil while a build for the same key is still running, so two requests/watch events build the SAME key concurrently — producing two distinct index instances where the caller holding the non-cached one never observes later writes (stale search results), and, for file-backed indices (size > FileThreshold), two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opening the same on-disk directory. HOW: guard the build per key (e.g. re-check the cache under the write lock after acquiring it, or use a per-key single-flight/lock so only one build runs per NamespacedResource), rather than relying on a global write lock held for the entire body.

The cache mutex was moved to cover only the cache assignment, removing the serialization that previously surrounded the whole BuildIndex. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can now both construct an index (including `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same on-disk path) and both write `b.cache[key]`; the second overwrites the first, so callers get distinct index instances for one key and writes made through the losing instance are invisible to readers of the cached one (and the file-backed build may collide on the same directory). Keep the build for a given key serialized (e.g. restore the lock around the build, or take a per-key lock) instead of locking only the map write.

Locking only cache publication allows concurrent requests for the same uncached key to build separate indexes and overwrite each other's cache entries. Search and handleEvent both call getOrCreateIndex, whose GetIndex previously blocked behind the build-wide lock; now an event can update one newly built index before another build replaces it, losing that update from subsequent search results and leaving the discarded index open. Serialize builds per NamespacedResource and recheck the cache after acquiring that per-key guard.

issues.descricao: The new startup log calls TotalDocs, which iterates the index cache without a lock, after the event goroutine that can add indexes has started, so a concurrent map read and write can crash the process.
issues.textoGolden: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

comentarios.texto: The newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call is unsafe: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-150) iterates `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`, while the bleve.go hunk in this same PR keeps `cacheMu` for the `b.cache[key] = idx` write only. Because search.go:207-213 already started the watch-event goroutine that can call `build` → `BuildIndex` → cache write, line 216 can iterate the map concurrently with that write, causing a `concurrent map iteration and map write` panic or data race. Either guard the `TotalDocs` read with `cacheMu`, or move this call to a point where no build can run concurrently.

The new startup log calls TotalDocs after launching the write-event listener, but bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu.RLock. A write event for an unindexed resource can concurrently publish an index through BuildIndex, causing a map iteration/write race and potentially a fatal runtime error during initialization. Protect TotalDocs cache iteration with the same read lock used by GetIndex.

BuildIndex now writes b.cache under Lock while TotalDocs (called from search.init after the watch goroutine starts) ranges over b.cache without any lock. This can cause a concurrent map read/write fatal error. Fix by taking cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

issues.descricao: NewResourceServer returns an error when Init fails without cancelling the server context created earlier.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and, on error, returns `nil, err` without invoking the `cancel` func created at line 229 and without running any lifecycle cleanup. WHY: Init may have already started long-lived goroutines — searchSupport.init's event-consumption loop uses context.Background() (resource/search.go:202) and initWatcher starts a watcher bound to s.ctx (server.go:752-770) — so if search.init succeeds and initWatcher (or a later step) fails, the constructor discards the server while those goroutines keep running with no way to stop them, leaking the internal context and watcher goroutines. HOW: on the error path call `cancel()` (and any needed lifecycle.Stop) before returning, or defer the cancel until success.

WHAT: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously but returns nil,err without calling the cancel created for s.ctx. WHY: Failed startup leaks the server context (and any lifecycle/watch resources partially started by Init), leaving goroutines/channel watches alive. HOW: On Init error call s.cancel() (and lifecycle Stop cleanup) before returning.

issues.descricao: The PR skips the storage-server module integration test on postgres instead of fixing the failure, removing coverage of the new eager initialization on postgres.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The new user-mismatch check reads integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without verifying that the 'sender' key exists. WHY: Integrations that pre-date this metadata field or were created without the installation webhook will raise KeyError and crash the installation pipeline instead of showing the intended error page. HOW: Use a safe lookup for the sender login and treat a missing sender as an unverifiable request.

The `error_short` strings (`"Invalid installation request."`, `"GitHub installation pending deletion."`, `"Github installed on another Sentry organization."`) are user-facing messages, but they are passed as plain string literals to `error()` rather than being wrapped in `_()`. Because they are only used inside the function as `_(error_short)`, gettext extraction tools cannot discover them, so they will never be translated. Define module-level constants for these short messages wrapped in `_()`, and use those constants as the default and call-site values (mirroring how `error_long` already uses `ERR_INTEGRATION_*` constants).

issues.descricao: error() calls _(error_short) on a variable and callers pass plain literals, so the short error strings are no longer extractable for translation.

comentarios.texto: The helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. The translation extractor cannot see these strings, so the short error messages sent to the user are no longer translatable; the old code wrapped the literals directly in `_()`. Mark the literals with gettext_lazy at the call sites and the default, and pass them through without wrapping again.

error_short strings bypass translation extraction: _(error_short) uses a variable so makemessages cannot collect them. Wrap literals at definition/call sites, e.g. error_short=_("Invalid installation request.") and pass _("...") literals, then use data error value directly without re-wrapping.

Translate the short-message literals at their definition/call sites instead of calling `_(error_short)` on a variable. Django's message extraction cannot extract the default `"Invalid installation request."` or the plain-string arguments at the two call sites from this dynamic gettext invocation. The existing pending-deletion and already-installed messages previously appeared directly inside `_()`; this refactor removes their extraction sites, and the new default message cannot enter translation catalogs. Use a translated default and translated arguments, then place `error_short` directly into the payload so these user-facing errors remain localizable.

issues.descricao: The org parameter of error()/get_document_origin is actually the active-organization context, not an Organization, so the name is misleading.

comentarios.texto: The parameter is named `org` but the code treats it as the pipeline's active-organization context: it dereferences `org.organization` and every caller (error() and the GitHubInstallation sites) passes `self.active_organization`, not an Organization. The name misstates the argument's type/contract — a caller following the name and passing a real Organization would hit AttributeError on `.organization`. Rename the parameter (e.g. `active_organization`) and correct the corresponding name in `error()` at line 131 so the two signatures match what is actually passed.

issues.descricao: The GitHub OAuth state is pipeline.signature, a static md5 of the pipeline view names, instead of a per-attempt random nonce, so it gives no CSRF protection.
issues.textoGolden: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

comentarios.texto: The OAuth state is pipeline.signature, which Pipeline.__init__ computes solely from pipeline view class names and therefore shares across all users and installation attempts. An attacker can obtain an OAuth code for their own GitHub account and send a callback using this known state to a victim with an active installation pipeline, binding the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's flow instead of rejecting the forged callback. Generate a random per-attempt nonce, store it in pipeline state, and validate that nonce on the OAuth callback.

Do not use pipeline.signature as OAuth state. It is a deterministic MD5 of the pipeline identifiers, not an unpredictable nonce tied to this user's authorization attempt (the tests reuse it across users). An attacker can know the expected state and submit a callback containing a code authorized under the attacker's GitHub account, defeating the OAuth login-CSRF protection and the intended binding to the installing user. Generate a cryptographically random per-attempt state, store it in the session/pipeline, and validate and consume it on callback.

issues.descricao: The new OAuth step's token exchange and user lookup are not wrapped in error handling, so GitHub/network failures surface as 500s instead of the installation-failed page.

comentarios.texto: The token request is executed outside the try block. If GitHub's token endpoint is unavailable or the request fails with a connection/timeout error, safe_urlopen raises before the guarded response parsing is reached, and this new installation step returns an unhandled server error instead of the installation-failed response. Include the request itself in the error handling and handle the relevant transport exceptions.

WHAT: safe_urlopen token exchange and get_user_info() (which calls resp.raise_for_status()) are called with no exception handling. WHY: Any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from GitHub bubbles up as an unhandled exception and 500s the install instead of rendering the invalid-request page. HOW: Wrap the exchange plus get_user_info in try/except and return error() on failure.

safe_urlopen() and get_user_info() are called outside any try/except, so network errors, non-2xx responses, or API failures raise unhandled exceptions instead of returning error(). Wrap the token exchange + user-info fetch in try/except and return error() on failure, matching the handled missing-access_token path.

issues.descricao: When no Integration exists yet for the installation_id the pipeline advances without comparing the OAuth user to the installer, bypassing the new ownership check.

comentarios.texto: The missing Integration branch advances the pipeline without verifying that github_authenticated_user installed the supplied installation_id. When the installation webhook has not created a record, or the local record was deleted, finish_pipeline calls build_integration using app credentials and attaches the installation without checking the OAuth user's access, allowing a user with another account's installation ID to bypass the new ownership check. Fail closed until trusted installer information is available and apply the ownership check before every successful next_step.

The record-absent path advances the pipeline before checking whether the authenticated GitHub user installed this app. Installation IDs arrive from the request, and a missing Integration record (for example before the installation webhook is processed) does not establish ownership. As a result, this path can attach an installation belonging to a different GitHub user despite the new authenticity check. Verify the authenticated user's authorization for the installation before advancing in this branch too, rather than relying on the webhook-created record existing.

When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the code calls next_step() without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the installer. An attacker can supply an installation_id they do not own before the installation webhook has created the row, and bypass the new verification. Do not skip the check in this branch. Either fail closed, or verify ownership another way, for example by confirming the user can access the installation through the GitHub API.

issues.descricao: The installer check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking that sender exists, raising KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.
issues.textoGolden: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

comentarios.texto: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is indexed without checking that "sender" exists, so an ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender raises KeyError (500) here. metadata["sender"] is only populated when state.get("sender") is set (integration.py:376-377), and the only writer of that state is the installation webhook (webhook.py:202-208); integrations created through the pipeline itself carry no sender (confirmed by installation.py:44 which explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`, and by the pipeline-created integration in test_integration.py:730-743). Previously this branch only bound state and called pipeline.next_step(), so this crash is newly introduced. Fix: guard the lookup, e.g. `if pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != (integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login"):` and decide the desired fallback when sender is absent.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError. build_integration (line 376-377) only sets metadata["sender"] when state.get("sender") is truthy, so an existing Integration without a sender entry makes this subscripting throw an unhandled KeyError (500) instead of routing to the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and treat a missing sender as a failed verification) so the mismatch/absence case returns error() rather than crashing.

The new ownership check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] even though GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration omits sender for normal pipeline-created integrations. Reconnecting an existing active integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without webhook-populated sender now raises KeyError and returns a server error rather than an installation failure. Handle missing sender explicitly and return the invalid-installation response when trusted installer metadata is unavailable.

issues.descricao: test_installation_not_found uses a wrong OAuth state, so it fails at the state check and never reaches the installation-not-found path it is meant to test.

comentarios.texto: First response (installation_id) is overwritten by second response (bad state) with no assertion, so the Integration.DoesNotExist / not-ACTIVE branch in GitHubInstallation is never verified. Keep/assert the first flow through a valid OAuth step to reach the installation check instead of only asserting the OAuth state-mismatch error.

This test no longer verifies the "installation not found" path it exists for. The second GET supplies state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the github pipeline signature (that is the 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 asserted in test_github_setup and reused elsewhere). OAuthLoginView.dispatch (integration.py:412-413) therefore returns error() before GitHubInstallation runs, producing the same generic "Invalid installation request." message and the same failed template via the state-mismatch branch. The Integration.DoesNotExist handling at integration.py:493-498 is never reached, so the test would still pass if that handling were removed or broken. Use the real pipeline state so the request advances into GitHubInstallation, or assert on something that distinguishes the state-mismatch branch from the missing-installation branch.

The replacement assertion no longer verifies that a nonexistent installation is rejected: 'Invalid installation request.' is also returned for a state mismatch, missing access token, or missing authenticated login before GitHubInstallation is reached. This test can therefore pass with installation-not-found handling broken if the callback fails OAuth validation instead. Establish a successful OAuth exchange with the actual pipeline state and verify that the nonexistent installation lookup is reached and rejected, rather than accepting this shared authentication-error message alone.
